text: The recycler has a bale of plastic ready to ship and the buyer backs out. Where does {name} expect that bale to go?
author: Codex writer B

text: It'll stay at the plant until somebody wants it, {presiding}. I'd still put a refund on the bottle. Right now there's nothing in it for the person who picks it up off the ground.
author: Codex writer B

text: Getting a bottle off the roadside is worth doing, {presiding}. Selling the material takes a buyer.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want the buyer's name before sending a load over there, {presiding}. If the sale falls through, the recycler has to find another bay in the warehouse.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's where I get stuck, {first}. The customer can collect the refund while the recycler still has a bale nobody will buy.
author: Codex writer B

text: Where would {name} put the first bag of returns in a grocery that barely has room for the stock it sells?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask whether the shop can share a return counter with a neighbor, {presiding}. I'd vote for the deposit and give a small store somewhere to send the empties.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd take {first} into the stockroom with the owner. If there's space for those bags between deliveries, the owner can show us where.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd have to move something out to make room, {presiding}. I'd count what the shop gives up before voting yes.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd walk through that stockroom with {first} and ask the owner what would have to come out. Until I see the space, I can't promise it's there.
author: Codex writer B

text: The students have been collecting bottles for their trip. What would {name} tell the club treasurer those bottles will bring once the refund ends?
author: Codex writer B

text: Get a price from the scrap yard, {presiding}. A club could still collect cans after repeal, but I'd hate to see the treasurer book a bus on the old refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: They'd lose the deposit income, {presiding}. I favor repeal, but I wouldn't promise those students their cans will bring the same money.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the refund, {first}. A treasurer who counts the bottles today can tell the class what they'll have for the trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the club bring its receipts in, {presiding}. Before taking the refund away I'd like the committee to see what that money bought last term.
author: Codex writer B

text: The grocer paid the last customer on time. How long does the store have to get its own money back, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: Give the grocer a filing date of its own, {presiding}. A clerk could pay a customer on the last afternoon and still need time to send the claim in.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd give the stores a chance to settle up, {presiding}. They need time to file after the last customer brings a bottle back.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's the date I'd want in writing, {first}. The shopper has already been paid. The grocer shouldn't have to get a truck there that same day to recover the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: I can't give {first} a date the dealer can rely on. That's why I'd keep the deposit until we know how those last claims will be paid.
author: Codex writer B

text: These drinks sit beside each other on the shelf. If only one carries a deposit, what can the cashier show the customer, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: Mark the bottle, {presiding}. Then the clerk can turn it in their hand and point out the refund without calling a manager.
author: Codex writer B

text: Start with what the shopper can see, {presiding}. If the label tells the drinks apart, put the refund there too.
author: Codex writer B

text: Put me at that counter with {first} and I couldn't explain why one counts and the other doesn't. I'd settle the list before handing the cashier the job.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd send the list back to committee, {presiding}. By the time the lid comes off, the shopper should already know what the empty bottle is worth.
author: Codex writer B

text: The distributor marks the bottles and the clerk counts them when they come back. Which of those jobs would {name} pay a handling allowance for?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd pay the store for taking returns, {presiding}. Let the distributor include the cost of marking the cases in what it charges to deliver them.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let both bring in their costs, {presiding}. Marking a case takes different work from counting loose bottles at the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: Show {first} what happens behind the counter when a bag comes in. Somebody has to count it, sort it and put it somewhere. I'd price that work before promising an allowance.
author: Codex writer B

text: Start with the clerk who sorts the bottles, {presiding}. If the distributor wants a share too, I'd ask what work the store hasn't already done.
author: Codex writer B

text: Say I pay the deposit on my way home tonight and the refund ends tomorrow. What happens when I finally empty the bottle, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd let {first} bring that empty back. Set a final return day far enough out to finish the drink, and put it up on the shelf while people are still buying.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd stop charging the deposit on new sales and keep the return counter open for the old bottles, {presiding}. Those shoppers have already paid.
author: Codex writer B

text: Finish the drink and take the bottle back, {first}. That's the promise the store made at the till, and it's one reason I'd keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the store can take my deposit Friday and turn me away Saturday, {presiding}, I'm voting to keep the return counter open.
author: Codex writer B

text: Where would {name} send a family with a box of glass if the store stops taking returns and the town leaves glass at the curb?
author: Codex writer B

text: A county drop-off might take them, {presiding}. Before we print directions, let's find out which sites actually handle glass.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd have each county name the site that will take the glass, {presiding}. Read those names against the list of towns and see who would be left without one.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want to give {first} directions from the grocery to a place that actually takes glass. Right now a family can get that job done when they buy food.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the store counter, {presiding}. Until somebody can name a nearby place that takes glass, we're sending that family home with the same box.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd vote for {issue}. Let one truck take the distributors' empties together and the grocer can use that stockroom again.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm with the member, {presiding}. Let's hear from the corner shops about where a shared return counter could go.
author: Codex writer B

text: Print the refund on the bottle, {presiding}. Then the shopper knows what it's worth before carrying it to the store. I'd vote for that.
author: Codex writer B

text: A shop could pay a refund on a water bottle that came in on somebody else's route. I'd like {name} to tell that grocer who'll pay the money back before I vote yes.
author: Codex writer B

text: Stand behind a customer with a sack of cans and one clerk at the till, {presiding}. That's why I'm voting no.
author: Codex writer B

text: Give the bottlers until we meet again, {presiding}. If they can keep the roadsides clear themselves, I'd like to see them do it before we start collecting deposits.
author: Codex writer B

text: I share that doubt, {presiding}. I'd want to see a buyer for the plastic before asking stores to collect it this way.
author: Codex writer B

text: Before I could support {issue}, I'd want a bottler to trace the trip back from the store to the washer. There's little use saving refillables if we can't get them home.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who pays the clerk while the empties are being counted and sorted? I'm with {name} on holding off until the store knows whose payroll covers that time.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd vote for {issue} if people could collect the refund anywhere that sells that kind of drink. How many shoppers remember where a loose bottle came from?
author: Codex writer B

text: Show the refund mark on the label, {presiding}. A confusing package is something we can fix without giving up the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd give {issue} a chance. Could the distributors share a pickup so the store doesn't have to wait on each truck?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd end it too, {presiding}. A grocer could use that room for groceries again.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'll vote to end the deposit. I'm reserving judgment on when a shop should have to file its last claim.
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, end the deposit. I'd give people time to bring back bottles they've already paid on.
author: Codex writer B

text: Until you can tell a family where else to take glass on a grocery trip, I'd keep taking bottles at the store.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep it, {presiding}. A club collecting cans can count on the refund when it plans a field trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: Why throw the refund out? I'd hear the grocer out on what the store gets paid for handling bottles.
author: Codex writer B

text: I agree, {presiding}. Someone who paid the deposit ought to decide when to bring the bottle back.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm wary of taking the grocery off the return route. A county site can be a long drive.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the refund too, {presiding}. A bag of cans is worth carrying home when you know what you'll get for it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd let the shopkeeper have the stockroom back. That's enough for me to vote for repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: We can stop charging on new bottles and still honor the old ones. Give people that chance and I'll vote to end the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd end the refund, {presiding}, and ask which county sites take glass. I'd want those addresses posted before the last return day.
author: Codex writer B

text: A shared pickup gets the cases out of the store. Now which company credits the grocer for the refunds already paid on those cases?
author: Codex writer B

text: Walk that route with a corner-shop owner before choosing the shared counter. Would somebody carrying a sack from the store actually make that trip?
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you, {presiding}. A parent buying juice ought to be able to tell right there in the aisle what the empty is worth.
author: Codex writer B

text: Could the distributors settle those claims together? Somebody returning a water bottle has no way to tell us which truck delivered it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let's hear from the clerk who has to deal with the sack of cans at lunchtime. What limit would keep the till open and still let that customer collect a refund?
author: Codex writer B

text: And when we meet again? If the bottlers come back asking for another season, what would make you say they've had their chance?
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the recycler bring the purchase order, {first}. A picture of the plastic piled up outside won't tell us whether anybody has agreed to take it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd put the trip back to the filling plant on that map, {presiding}. An empty takes up room on a truck too.
author: Codex writer B

text: Exactly, {presiding}. A store can't make payroll with the deposit it hands back to a customer.
author: Codex writer B

text: Say the customer gets the money and the bottle stays at the store. I'd still want to know who owes the shop if it never carried that brand.
author: Codex writer B

text: A printer can put on a mark once we tell the printer which drinks qualify. Where would you draw that line?
author: Codex writer B

text: Would that truck take everybody's bottles on the same day, {presiding}? A grocer needs to know when the space will be clear.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. When the last load leaves, that room is worth something to the store even if it never sells another bottle.
author: Codex writer B

text: Fair enough. Before setting the last day a store can file, I'd hear from the people who check the claims.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd put the last return date on the store door while people still have time to bring their bottles in.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose the county took glass at the grocery, {first}. Would that answer your objection to repeal, or do you want the shopper to get the deposit back as well?
author: Codex writer B

text: What would the scrap yard pay the club? I'd like to see that beside the refund before we decide what ending the refund would mean for the next trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who would send the handling payment to the store? I'd hate to tell a shopkeeper we've settled it when nobody can say who writes the check.
author: Codex writer B

text: A family that buys drinks by the case may still have full bottles on the shelf when stores stop charging the deposit. Thank you for bringing them up.
author: Codex writer B

text: How far is the round trip from the edge of the county, {presiding}? That's what I'd put beside the address.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's why I'd keep the refund. A kid picking up cans shouldn't need to follow the scrap market to know whether the trip is worth it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a regular pickup clear enough room for that shopkeeper? I'd try it before taking the refund away from everybody who shops there.
author: Codex writer B

text: After stores stop collecting the deposit, how will the clerk tell an old bottle from one sold after the change if the packages still look alike?
author: Codex writer B

text: Post the address, {presiding}, but walk the route before you send anyone there. How is a shopper on foot supposed to carry glass from the grocery to the county site?
author: Codex writer B

text: Give an empty can a refund and a school club can collect it for the trip fund. The club can work out what a bag is worth before anybody goes knocking. That's why I'm voting for {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: {presiding}, a grocer has every right to ask who'll take the bottles away. Distributors can share that pickup. I want us to make the return trip work, and I'll vote for the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: When you pay a deposit, you ought to be able to walk back into a store with your empties and get it back. That's the promise I'd vote to make with {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: If we put a deposit on a drink, somebody buying it ought to know at the shelf whether they can claim a refund. I support {bill-name}, and I want that clear before the first bottle comes back.
author: Codex writer B

text: {presiding}, imagine running a corner grocery. Where would you put a day's worth of returns while you wait for a truck? That space has to come from somewhere. I'll vote against {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: A grocer can mark the minutes a clerk spends counting bottles. What goes on the distributor's claim? I'd hold my vote, {presiding}, until I see what we're paying each of them to do.
author: Codex writer B

text: I can see how a bottle gets from the store to the recycler. What happens if the recycler has a warehouse full and no buyer for the plastic? I can't support {bill-name} with that question open.
author: Codex writer B

text: Look at the drink cases the way a cashier sees them, {presiding}. Same size bottle, same cap. If only one carries a refund, I'd want the cashier to have something to go by besides the flavor.
author: Codex writer B

text: Consider a grocer who stores returns in the stockroom. I'd give the owner that space back. That's space the owner could use for groceries again. I'd end the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: I favor ending the deposit. Before we set the last return day, I want the grocer who pays the last customer a refund to know where to send the claim.
author: Codex writer B

text: We can end the deposit and still give people time to bring back the bottles they paid it on. Set a last return date people can plan around and I'll vote for repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm for repeal, {presiding}. A family with a box of glass will still need somewhere to take it. I'd like the collection arrangements in people's hands before the refunds end.
author: Codex writer B

text: If a school club pays for trips with cans, what do we tell the kids when the store stops paying the refund? They'd have to start by asking what a scrap dealer would pay. I'd keep the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: A refillable already has a long trip back to the plant to be washed. Why take away the refund that gets it as far as the counter? I'm voting against repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: Think about the bottles in somebody's pantry, {presiding}. They paid the deposit at the register. I don't want their chance to get it back to depend on whether they hear about the cutoff. I'm against repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: A shopper can walk a bag of bottles back to the corner store. If the closest collection site left is outside town, how does somebody without a car get there? I want to keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Bring the driver and the grocer to the same table, {presiding}. I'd vote to start collecting deposits. Before we divide the handling money, I want to hear what it costs to pick up a load and what it costs to get one ready.
author: Codex writer B

text: A bottle that can be washed and filled again is worth getting back to the bottler, {presiding}. With a refund waiting at the counter, there's a reason to carry the empty in. I'll vote yes.
author: Codex writer B

text: At the register a customer ought to be able to ask which drinks carry the deposit and get a straight answer. I think we can manage that. I ask the chamber to pass {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Give the shop that barely has room for groceries a partner to take returns, {presiding}. I'd vote to start the deposit and help the stores find a collection counter their customers can reach.
author: Codex writer B

text: The bottlers say they can get the empties off the roadside themselves. Give them until we meet again, {presiding}. When we come back I want to see the road they picked.
author: Codex writer B

text: A clerk working alone can't leave the lunch line to count a customer's whole sack of cans. I'd need some leeway for the little stores, {presiding}, before I could vote for a deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: The water delivery routes overlap, {presiding}. A store could hand back money on another distributor's bottles all week. I'd want that store paid before I voted to start collecting deposits.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm looking at this from the loading dock, {presiding}. A driver with a mixed load ought to know whose empties can ride. I'd want that settled before stores have to start taking them.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd be glad to see the end of the argument at the counter over which bottle qualifies. I'd vote to end the deposit. Give customers fair notice about the empties they already have.
author: Codex writer B

text: For the clerk alone at the register, a bag of empties is a job to do while the lunch line waits. That's who I've got in mind as I vote to end the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: A refund brings back the plastic. It can't guarantee a buyer for what piles up at the recycling plant. I'm ready to end the deposit. We'll still need an answer from the people buying that plastic.
author: Codex writer B

text: I support repeal. A club that raises trip money with cans needs to know what becomes of its next collection. The scrap dealer may pay less. The kids deserve to know that while there's still time to plan.
author: Codex writer B

text: Change the handling fee if the stores are coming up short. Why take the refund away from the person who brings the bottle back? I'll vote to keep it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who carries the cost of the last refund while a dealer waits for the distributor to settle up? I'd keep the deposit. If the chamber ends it, I want that dealer's claim honored.
author: Codex writer B

text: If similar bottles get different treatment, let's clear up which ones qualify. A customer shouldn't have to give up a refund to get a clearer label. That's why I'm voting to keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd rather put the grocer and the distributor at this table, {presiding}, and hear what each trip costs. We can revisit their allowances and keep paying customers for bringing the containers back.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the recycler showed us a signed order for the plastic, would that satisfy {name}, or would the plant need a second buyer in case the order falls through?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want another outlet, {first}. One canceled shipment can leave the recycler renting room for bales it thought would be on the road by now.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let me see when the buyer can turn a shipment down, {presiding}. A signature doesn't clear the warehouse if slow sales let the customer cancel.
author: Codex writer B

text: The stockroom is a good place to start. What would you ask {hearing-opponent} about freeing up space while the refund is still in effect?
author: Codex writer B

text: Whether a shared pickup would clear enough room between deliveries. I'd put the same question to {hearing-supporter} and compare what each could find out from the grocers.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask for a pickup schedule from a shop that runs out of room. That would help us decide whether to change {bill-name} or leave it as filed.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you send the dealer's last claim to {hearing-opponent} to see where a store could get stuck waiting for its money?
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes. Ask {hearing-supporter} to follow the claim from the distributor's side. Have both mark where they'd expect to see a receipt.
author: Codex writer B

text: Use {bill-name} as it stands when you send it. If the store can't tell who settles its claim by reading the bill, we have more to write.
author: Codex writer B

text: Which part of the last refund would you ask {hearing-supporter} to trace for the committee?
author: Codex writer B

text: The handoff at the loading dock. Then let {hearing-opponent} check whether the count on the driver's ticket matches what the dealer paid out.
author: Codex writer B

text: The trip from the register to the reimbursement check. If there's a gap, I'd like it marked in the margin of {bill-name} before we vote.
author: Codex writer B

text: Before we set the last return day in {bill-name}, who would you ask to try it out with a bag of empties?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask {hearing-opponent} to take the shopper's part. Where would someone find the date on a bottle bought before repeal?
author: Codex writer B

text: Give {hearing-supporter} the receipt and the proposed date. See whether a person who bought the drinks last week would know how long they had.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you send the proposed notice to {hearing-opponent} before you settle on a deadline?
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes. I'd send it to {hearing-supporter} as well. I want to know what each thinks a cashier should do with a customer who shows up on the last afternoon.
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, with the draft of {bill-name} beside it. Someone reading only the notice should get the same last return day as someone reading the bill.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you ask {hearing-supporter} to check where the glass could go before stores stop paying refunds?
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, and I'd ask {hearing-opponent} to try those directions from a grocery store on foot. A site can take glass and still be out of reach for a shopper.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want the site operator to confirm what it takes. I wouldn't put a collection site into the notice for {bill-name} on the strength of a street address alone.
author: Codex writer B

text: Which sign would you show {hearing-opponent} first, the price on the shelf or the notice at the return counter?
author: Codex writer B

text: The shelf tag. I'd hand the return notice to {hearing-supporter} and ask them to read the signs together as a customer would.
author: Codex writer B

text: The return notice. If it says people have longer than {bill-name} actually allows, the cashier will have to answer for that at the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: The committee heard {hearing-supporter} on the bill. What would you want checked at the register before you promise the clerk a shorter line?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want a timed count with customers waiting. Let {hearing-opponent} pick the time of day so we're also hearing what happens when the shop is busy.
author: Codex writer B

text: Whether the work actually goes away under {bill-name} or just moves to the afternoon when everyone brings the last bags in.
author: Codex writer B

text: If a distributor offered to take the bags directly, what would you need from {hearing-opponent} before you called that a fair trade for shoppers?
author: Codex writer B

text: A trip somebody could actually make without a car. Then I'd ask {hearing-supporter} whether the distributor would be open when that person got there.
author: Codex writer B

text: Directions a customer could use after work. I'd want that arrangement confirmed before voting to replace returns at the store under {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose we hear from {hearing-opponent} again. What would convince you a recycler could sell the bottles coming back?
author: Codex writer B

text: A buyer willing to take the next delivery as well as what's already baled. I'd ask {hearing-supporter} to read the cancellation terms with me.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want an order the recycler can ship against. I wouldn't change my vote on {bill-name} just because somebody found room to store more plastic.
author: Codex writer B

text: You've already said the club could get less for its cans. What would you ask {hearing-supporter} to bring back before the students set a trip price?
author: Codex writer B

text: A quote from the scrap yard for a load like the club's. I'd let {hearing-opponent} check that quote against what the club could collect in refunds now.
author: Codex writer B

text: An offer that says how long the price will hold. Before I support a deadline in {bill-name}, I want to know whether the club has time to collect and deliver the cans.
author: Codex writer B

text: What could we put in {bill-name} for a club that's collected the cans but hasn't turned them in yet?
author: Codex writer B

text: A final return period. I'd ask {hearing-opponent} to find out how much notice a sponsor needs to borrow a truck and get the bags to the store.
author: Codex writer B

text: A requirement to tell customers when the refund ends. I'd send {hearing-supporter} the proposed notice and ask where a student collecting cans would see it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Say the truck misses its last pickup. Who would you want to walk {hearing-supporter} through what stays on the grocer's floor?
author: Codex writer B

text: The receiver who signs for deliveries. I'd also invite {hearing-opponent} to see how much of that room the grocer gets back when the truck finally comes.
author: Codex writer B

text: Start with whoever holds the key to that stockroom. The day {bill-name} takes effect and the day the grocer gets the space back could be a long way apart.
author: Codex writer B

text: A box of glass is heavy. Who would you put beside {hearing-opponent} to work out that trip home from the store and on to the collection site?
author: Codex writer B

text: Someone who walks to buy groceries. I'd have {hearing-supporter} meet them at the store so we're talking about the same trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: The person who picks the site. Before a notice goes out under {bill-name}, that person should see the route a shopper would have to take.
author: Codex writer B

text: A cashier may still have a line of people carrying old bottles. What would you put at the door so a shopper could sort the empties if {bill-name} passes?
author: Codex writer B

text: Pictures of the containers the store still takes. Give {hearing-opponent} a bottle from the shelf and see whether the sign tells them what to do with it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Try it with {hearing-supporter} carrying a bottle that looks like one we've covered but never had a deposit. That's the awkward conversation the cashier has to get right.
author: Codex writer B

text: What's the first thing a buyer could show {hearing-supporter} that we couldn't learn by looking at a stack of bales?
author: Codex writer B

text: A delivery date. If there's an order, {hearing-opponent} could check when the plastic is actually supposed to leave the building.
author: Codex writer B

text: Whether the buyer will take the next load too. If we're relying on that sale to make a case for changing {bill-name}, we need more than an empty corner in the warehouse.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like to hear where {hearing-supporter} would look for the last return date. What about the people who've already bought their bottles?
author: Codex writer B

text: Those bottles could sit in a garage for weeks. I'd ask {hearing-supporter} to try finding the date from home before we settle on posting it in stores.
author: Codex writer B

text: The first time some people hear of {bill-name} could be when they bring the bottles back. I'd leave time between putting up the notice and closing the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: Two empties on the counter, both from the same fridge. Where in {bill-name} could the clerk point to explain why only one pays?
author: Codex writer B

text: Read the labels. Could {hearing-supporter} match each drink to a line on our notice? That's what the clerk will have to do.
author: Codex writer B

text: Give {hearing-opponent} the two labels and the notice we're proposing. If you still have to know the answer in advance, the clerk doesn't stand a chance.
author: Codex writer B

text: If {hearing-opponent} brings back a brand the grocer has never stocked, does your notice tell the clerk to turn it away?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd have the notice say which drinks still qualify. I'd want {hearing-opponent} to be able to read it without having to remember which store sold the bottle.
author: Codex writer B

text: A brand list could shut somebody out by mistake. While returns are still open, {bill-name} ought to tell the clerk whether the kind of drink is what counts.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose the grocer honors that notice down to the last minute. When would {bill-name} let the grocer turn in the bottles?
author: Codex writer B

text: The customer should get the whole last day. I'd ask {hearing-supporter} to follow the bottles from that last refund until the dealer can turn them over for payment.
author: Codex writer B

text: Two dates on the notice, please. I'd have {hearing-opponent} check which one a shopper would see first and print the dealer's instructions separately if it's confusing.
author: Codex writer B

text: What does a grocer do with another sack of empties when the truck is late, {presiding}? Something else has to come off the stockroom floor. That's why I'm voting to end the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: Give me a choice between a shelf for tomorrow's bread and a shelf for yesterday's bottles and I'll take the bread. The grocer could use that shelf again if we end the deposit. That's where I stand.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm backing {bill-name} for a pretty ordinary reason. A delivery driver ought to be able to get a hand truck through the back door without the clerk having to shift a stack of sticky bottles first.
author: Codex writer B

text: {presiding}, I'll vote to end the deposit. But who's holding the money when the last customer leaves? The shopper has a refund and the grocer has a bag of glass. We still owe that grocer a way to settle up.
author: Codex writer B

text: The shopper who brings back the last bottle isn't the last person owed money. Close the return counter, by all means. Keep the dealer's claim open long enough to get the money back into the till.
author: Codex writer B

text: I support {bill-name}. A grocer who pays the last refund out of the register should be able to hand in the claim the next morning and get paid.
author: Codex writer B

text: A refund is part of what a shopper pays for. Let people empty the bottles they bought while the deposit was still on them, {presiding}, and I'll gladly help close the books on it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Picture somebody buying a case the evening before repeal. I'd give that family time to drink it before they have to bring the bottles back. I'm ready to end the deposit on those terms.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who has a bag of empties by the back door right now? People kept those bottles because we told them they'd get their money back. I'll support {bill-name} and a return period that keeps our word.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd vote to end the refund, {presiding}. Glass still has to go somewhere. Try carrying a week's worth home again after finding out the grocery has stopped taking it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Set a box of bottles on the kitchen floor. Now tell somebody who walks to the store what to do with it when the return counter closes. I favor repeal and I want to be able to give that person directions.
author: Codex writer B

text: Of course I'll vote for {bill-name}. But if the grocery quits taking glass on Monday, where do I carry it on Tuesday? A town ought to have an answer before its counter closes.
author: Codex writer B

text: A clerk shouldn't have to referee an argument over two bottles that look alike. I support repeal, {presiding}. Let's give the people who paid deposits on those bottles time to find out what's changing.
author: Codex writer B

text: Same size bottle, same shelf, different answer at the register. I'd end the deposit. I'd like to see that argument end too. The shopper deserves to hear about the change before making a trip back.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm for {bill-name}. I can see why a shopper would be sore about saving a bag of bottles and finding out at the counter that some of them never carried a deposit. Let's at least give people fair warning.
author: Codex writer B

text: Think about a store with a single till, {presiding}. While the clerk is counting a sack of empties, the milk is sitting on the belt and nobody can pay for it. That's my vote for repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who covers the register while the clerk sorts the bottles? At a little grocery the answer might be nobody. I'd stop taking deposits and let the clerk get back to the lunch line.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd support {bill-name} on the small store alone. A bag of returns arrives just as the lunch rush starts. Which customer is the only clerk supposed to keep waiting?
author: Codex writer B

text: Will somebody buy the next bale, {presiding}? Paying to get bottles back can fill a shed with plastic before there's a buyer ready to use it. That's why I can vote to end the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: The refund gets a bottle as far as the plant. A buyer may need clean flakes, and all the plant has to sell is a bale. I wouldn't keep charging deposits on a promise the plant can't cash. I'm for repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: Line up a customer for the plastic and we've done something for recycling. Stack the bales in a warehouse and we've found a place to keep them. I'm supporting {bill-name} because a refund alone can't close that sale.
author: Codex writer B

text: A school club can count a refund before it books a bus, {presiding}. Scrap is worth what a buyer will pay that day, which may be less. I'm voting for repeal and I think the kids deserve to know that before they set the fare.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm for ending the deposit. Would I tell a club to keep collecting cans on the promise that the scrap will pay for the same trip? I wouldn't. They could come up short.
author: Codex writer B

text: Put yourself in the club treasurer's shoes. The cans are in a garage, the bus company wants a deposit, and the scrap price could leave you short. I support {bill-name}, but I'd tell the club that before it reserves the bus.
author: Codex writer B

text: Anybody who's unloaded a delivery knows you need somewhere to set the cases down. Even empty bottles take up that space. I'd end the deposit and let the grocer decide what goes in that space.
author: Codex writer B

text: Look behind the register, {presiding}. There's room to serve a customer or there's room for sacks waiting to go back. In a little store you may have to choose. I'd end the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: Where's the last refund coming from, {presiding}? The store pays it over the counter. Voting to end the deposit doesn't excuse us from seeing that money through to the dealer who advanced it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Picture the last return day at closing time. A customer gets a refund, the grocer puts the empties out back, the distributor hasn't come yet. I favor repeal and a chance for that grocer to collect.
author: Codex writer B

text: We promised a refund when those bottles went across the scanner. I'll vote to end the deposit, but anybody who took us at our word deserves a last chance to collect.
author: Codex writer B

text: If you knew the refund was ending, you'd bring the bottles back. What if you only buy groceries every other week? That's the shopper I want us to leave time for when we pass {bill-name}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Keep a place for the glass. That's my request to the members voting with me to end the deposit. Folks who hauled their bottles back to the store yesterday will still have bottles to carry tomorrow.
author: Codex writer B

text: Somebody who's been wheeling empties to the corner market in a shopping cart needs a place within reach. I'd pass {bill-name}, provided we do the work of showing people where their glass can go.
author: Codex writer B

text: A shopper saves an empty bottle in good faith and gets a lesson in beverage labels at the register. I can vote to end that, {presiding}. Give the shopper plenty of notice about what the store will still redeem.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm ready to stop charging deposits. Before the return counter closes, could we give the clerk something to point to when the customer says the bottle in this hand looks just like the one you took from the other?
author: Codex writer B

text: Behind a small counter, counting returns means putting the next sale on hold. I favor {bill-name} because that clerk only has one pair of hands.
author: Codex writer B

text: Imagine getting to the till with a sandwich and your bus pulling up outside. The clerk would love to take your money, but there's still a sack of cans to count. Give that store a break, {presiding}. I'll vote for repeal.
author: Codex writer B

text: A bale of plastic can sit under a roof for months. Until somebody orders it, have we really found a use for it? I'm voting for {bill-name} because collecting the bottles only gets us partway there.
author: Codex writer B

text: The plant can take another truckload, {presiding}. Can it sell what came in on the last one? That's the question the deposit leaves open for me, and it's why I'll vote to end it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Leave the trip money out of the club budget until somebody gets a scrap price. That's what I'd tell a student if the store stops paying the refund. I favor repeal, but I'd hate to see a kid promise the class a trip on the old refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Today a student can pick up an empty can and know what it's worth at the counter. After repeal it might fetch less at the yard. The trip still costs the club the same, {presiding}. I'll vote yes and give them fair warning.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd close the return counter too. The last time a driver takes those bags away, the grocer ought to get that corner back for good.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. I'd count a clear path from the loading door to the shelves as something the grocer gains when returns end.
author: Codex writer B

text: The floor space settles it for me, {presiding}. When the store fills up, the owner can't order a bigger back room.
author: Codex writer B

text: I appreciate that, {presiding}. A small shop has to make the deliveries and the returns fit through the same door.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep paying the refund. Give the distributors a common pickup day and see how much room the shop gets back.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you keep the refund even in a town where no distributor will take another one's empties? That's the shop I'd still want to give some relief by ending the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: I heard the point about room, {presiding}. I'd pay for more frequent pickups before I'd ask shoppers to give up the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who should cover that extra run, {presiding}? An empty truck going back past the store is one thing. Sending somebody out again is another.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd vote to close the return counter if the grocer can close out the last refund the same way a customer can. I don't want the store chasing a distributor for months.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's fair. I'll ask the committee to spell out the dealer's filing date before we vote.
author: Codex writer B

text: A separate deadline for the dealer makes sense, {presiding}. The shop can hardly file its last claim while the last customer is still at the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you, {presiding}. The dealer should have a chance to count what's in the bags and compare it with what went out of the till.
author: Codex writer B

text: A final claim worries me for a different reason. If a small shop has to advance the last refunds with no clear way to collect, I'll vote to keep the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a separate deadline for the dealer's claim answer that concern? A grocer could point to a date instead of waiting on a promise.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the refund, {presiding}. Settling up with dealers is something we can fix while customers still get their money back.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you back an end to new deposits if old claims were paid in full, {presiding}, or do you want to keep the charge on the next bottle too?
author: Codex writer B

text: The shopper paid on the way out. Give them time to get it back on the way in and I'll vote to stop charging deposits.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's the bargain I'd make with the shopper. Somebody who shops once a month ought to have a fair shot at making the trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm for repeal, {presiding}. But if a bottle is still unopened on somebody's pantry shelf, our notice has to reach them before the money runs out.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you, {presiding}. I'd start the return period when the public notice goes up. We shouldn't use it all up getting signs printed.
author: Codex writer B

text: I wouldn't end the refund. A last day is still a last day, and somebody who misses it is out the money they paid.
author: Codex writer B

text: How long would you give somebody to bring the empties back? I'd hear an argument for giving the shopper more time.
author: Codex writer B

text: What about people who put the empties aside until they have a ride? I'd keep the deposit, {presiding}. The last trip isn't equally easy for everybody.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose a shop took old returns until its regular customers had another chance to come in, {presiding}. Would that meet your concern?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd vote to end the deposit. Put the address of the nearest place that takes glass in the store window while people are still bringing bottles back.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. Before the return counter closes, I'd like somebody to take those directions from the store and check that the gate's open when they get there.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the county can take the glass, I'd let the shop out of the refund business. The store and the county both need to post the hours, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd add whether the site takes bottles from households, {presiding}. It's a long walk back with a box they won't accept.
author: Codex writer B

text: A place to drop off glass doesn't pay anybody back. I'd keep the refund even if the county takes glass right next door.
author: Codex writer B

text: So even with an easy trip, you'd keep the refund itself? That's a different reason to keep the counter open, and it's worth hearing.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the refund, {presiding}. Somebody who walks to the grocery may have no ride out to the county yard with a box of glass.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the county took glass where people already shop, {presiding}, would you still want the grocer to pay a refund?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm for ending the deposit. A shopper deserves to know which bottles the clerk will take before hauling a bag down to the store.
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes. I'd have the store post the last date and pictures of what still qualifies before the store stops taking returns.
author: Codex writer B

text: No clerk should have to break the news halfway through a bag of empties. I'd end the deposit and tell people first, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you, {presiding}. A sign on the way out reaches somebody buying a drink as well as somebody bringing one back.
author: Codex writer B

text: The trouble is that two bottles look alike. Give the clerk a clear label to show the customer and keep the refund. I'd vote to keep it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would that label help somebody with older bottles already at home? That's the shopper I want us to remember when we set the last return date.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd vote to keep it, {presiding}. People who saved the right containers shouldn't lose a refund because some other bottle looks just like theirs.
author: Codex writer B

text: During the changeover I'd have the clerk honor the qualifying bottles, {presiding}. Would you still charge the deposit on the next case sold?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd let the grocery close the return counter. Anybody who's next in line should be able to buy lunch while the last customer's cans are being counted.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. I'd let the clerk finish the sale and give the people still holding empties clear instructions on where to take them.
author: Codex writer B

text: The smallest store has the hardest time sparing a clerk. I'd end the refund, {presiding}, and give the store time to tell its customers.
author: Codex writer B

text: I agree on the notice, {presiding}. The person alone at the register will be the one hearing from people who missed it.
author: Codex writer B

text: A lunch line wouldn't make me give up the refund. Let a small shop limit how many containers it takes from one customer at a time.
author: Codex writer B

text: What limit would still make the trip worth a shopper's while? Before we end the deposit, I'd like an answer for the person carrying the bag too.
author: Codex writer B

text: The clerk's time costs money. I'd pay the shop for the work and keep the deposit, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a handling payment buy the store enough help at lunchtime, {presiding}? I'd have the shop price a shift before we count on it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd stop charging the deposit. Taking back another bottle doesn't do much good if the last load of plastic has nowhere to go.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you. If a buyer will take a shipment, I'd like to know in what form. We'll still need that answer after the return counter closes.
author: Codex writer B

text: I agree, {presiding}. A warehouse full of bales won't pay the plant's workers. Somebody has to want that plastic.
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, {presiding}. A real order tells the plant whether it's worth running another load through the grinder.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the buyer wants clean plastic, a refund could help bring it in sorted. I'd try that before I'd end the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: Which buyer would take it on those terms? Even if we keep the refund, the plant still needs somebody willing to pay for that plastic.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep collecting the bottles while the plant looks for customers, {presiding}. Stop now and the material won't be there when a buyer calls.
author: Codex writer B

text: How long should the plant keep taking loads without an order, {presiding}? I'd like to know who carries that cost.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm ready to end the deposit. Tell the club to get a price on the cans before anybody promises what they'll take off the cost of the trip.
author: Codex writer B

text: I appreciate that. I'd ask the committee to let clubs know the refund is ending while they still have time to change what they charge.
author: Codex writer B

text: The students ought to hear this before they book the bus, {presiding}. I'd support repeal and give them time to cash in what they've collected.
author: Codex writer B

text: Thank you, {presiding}. A last return day they can put on the school calendar would give the club a chance to get the bags to the store.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the refund for those kids. A club can plan around the refund. It can't book a trip on a price the scrap yard might offer next spring.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you still vote to keep the refund if the club could turn in this year's collection first? I'd like to know whether it's this trip or the one after it you're worried about.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the deposit, {presiding}. A club just getting started ought to have the same chance to raise money as the students who have cans saved already.
author: Codex writer B

text: Then your concern is next year's students as well as this year's bags, {presiding}. What would a club need in place before it could give up the refund?
author: Codex writer B

text: Before I could vote to close the return counter, I'd want to see how much space a joint pickup would actually free. If the grocer could get that room back and keep taking returns, I'd keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's worth measuring. But if the bags still block the next delivery, would you let that store stop taking empties then?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want one more answer about the dealer's last claim, {presiding}. I'd keep the deposit until a store can find out who will pay it when a distributor disputes the count.
author: Codex writer B

text: Do you need a name to send the claim to, {presiding}, or a way to appeal if the distributor turns it down?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd hold off on setting a last day for returns. A shopper who buys a case today may put it away for company. I'd want to know how that person ever hears there's a clock running on the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would it help to put the last return date beside the price while that case is still on the shelf? I'd put that notice in the proposal before the vote.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the refund for now, {presiding}. I wouldn't send anyone away from the grocery with a box of glass until somebody has tried the trip to the collection site on foot.
author: Codex writer B

text: Could we go together, {presiding}? I'd want to make that walk carrying bottles, at the time the grocery normally takes returns.
author: Codex writer B

text: It's the bottles already at home that worry me. Will the change be any easier to explain to somebody who already saved the bottles? Until I can answer that, I'd keep paying the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Could we try the proposed notice with a customer before we set the last return date? I'd like to see which bottle they expect the clerk to take.
author: Codex writer B

text: I can see the line at the register, {presiding}. Before I take away the refund, I'd want to hear whether the smallest shop could manage a shorter count per customer.
author: Codex writer B

text: What happens to the customer who's waited in line with more bottles than the store will count, {presiding}? I'd like to settle that before asking the shops to try it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd hold off on ending the deposit. If the buyer wants the plastic washed and ground, the trouble could be what we're offering for sale. I'd keep collecting bottles while the plant gets an answer.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would you ask the buyer to price a load in that condition? That's something the plant could take to the committee while we still have time to keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: A scrap price that could change by spring doesn't persuade me to end the deposit. I'd stick with the refund until the club knows what it can promise the students.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a written offer good through the club's collection day give the club enough certainty, or do you want next year's students to have the same guarantee?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the refund, {presiding}. A driver can take an empty case back only if somebody has filled it with empties.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's why I'd keep paying people to return those bottles. The bottler can arrange the whole trip from the store to the wash line and still have nothing to pick up.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd end the deposit. Getting glass as far as the store leaves the most expensive stretch of that trip ahead.
author: Codex writer B

text: It does, {presiding}. Would the member keep a refund on bottles a plant actually wants back if the bottler arranged the pickup?
author: Codex writer B

text: The customer gets the empty bottle as far as the store. What would convince {name} there's a truck going from there to a plant that can wash it?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask the bottler where the truck goes after its last delivery, {presiding}. If the plant takes that bottle and the truck goes back there, we've got a route worth discussing.
author: Codex writer B

text: The member has me on the first leg, {presiding}. Leave the bottle at home and the rest of that route doesn't matter.
author: Codex writer B

text: Exactly. Before we take away the refund I'd like us to stand at the loading door and ask what the driver would find there tomorrow.
author: Codex writer B

text: Even with a plant ready to refill the glass, I'd end the deposit. Somebody still has to haul all that weight home.
author: Codex writer B

text: Fair point, {presiding}. I'd ask what it costs to carry empties on a truck that's already headed there before we write the trip off.
author: Codex writer B

text: Does keeping the refund get the bottle washed, {presiding}, or does the store still need a bottler willing to take that particular glass?
author: Codex writer B

text: Somebody still has to haul the empties, {first}. A plant can offer to wash every bottle we send and the glass can still pile up behind the store.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep that walk to the corner store, {presiding}. A county address isn't much help to a shopper on foot.
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes. Before we move the collection point, I'd like somebody to make the round trip carrying a week's glass and tell us what the new arrangement asks of people.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd still stop charging the deposit. Could the county collect glass at the grocery where the shopper already walks?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd welcome a collection point at the grocery, {first}. Who's coming to haul the glass away before the next shopper finds it full?
author: Codex writer B

text: What counts as a return site for someone who walks to the grocery, {presiding}? A place that looks close on a map could be a long way with a bag of glass.
author: Codex writer B

text: A place they can actually walk to with the empties, {presiding}. I'd ask where the entrance is and when it's open before handing out directions.
author: Codex writer B

text: Before the last return claim is closed, I'd give the grocer time to put in that last claim too.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's the time I mean, {presiding}. A customer can leave with the refund at closing and the grocer can still be out the money when the shop opens.
author: Codex writer B

text: A dealer's last claim can survive repeal, {presiding}. I'd vote to end the deposit and leave time for the paperwork.
author: Codex writer B

text: Then I'd like to see a separate filing date for stores in writing. What does the store send in, and who still has authority to pay it?
author: Codex writer B

text: A pickup truck comes after the last return day. Which record would {name} use to decide whether the grocer gets paid?
author: Codex writer B

text: The dealer's record of paying the customer, {presiding}. A truck that collects the empties later shouldn't make an otherwise timely refund too late to claim.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the refund too. The club knows the refund before it promises anybody a seat on that bus.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's what the students can build a budget on, {presiding}. A scrap yard can quote a price today without promising it for the day the club sells.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd let the deposit end. The club can still collect cans and ask a yard what they're worth before booking anything.
author: Codex writer B

text: It can, {presiding}. Would you tell the students to set a fare from today's quote if their collection lasts until spring?
author: Codex writer B

text: The club treasurer has bags of cans and a trip to budget for. Once refunds end, what can go in the income column, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: Until there's a buyer, {presiding}, I'd count bags and leave the income line open. I'd hate for a kid to promise the class a trip the club can't pay for.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep the deposit, {presiding}. A full bottle at home is money somebody already expects to get back.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's the family I'd ask about setting a last return day. If they saved the case for company, the drinks may still be unopened on the day returns end.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd end the deposit if the old bottles still qualify for a time. A family can get its money back after stores quit charging the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: That might work, {presiding}. How will the family hear about the cutoff before it gets around to opening the case?
author: Codex writer B

text: The store posts the last return day beside the drinks. Would {name} give a family time to finish the case it bought before the sign went up?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd want both, {presiding}. If the family's next shopping day falls after the cutoff, seeing the sign then does them no good.
author: Codex writer B

text: I could vote to pay the store differently, {presiding}. I don't see why that should cost the shopper a refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: That's a change I'd sit down to write. If we end the refund altogether, it's the person bringing the empty back who loses money.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd vote to end the deposit. Changing a handling allowance still leaves the shop counting every bottle.
author: Codex writer B

text: It does, {presiding}. Would paying the full cost of the clerk's time change your mind about keeping the customer's refund?
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose we change what stores get for handling the empties. Which payment would {name} protect for the person who bought the drink?
author: Codex writer B

text: At the counter, {presiding}. The store can get a different amount for its work while the shopper still collects what they paid on the drink.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep paying the refund. Let's put the two bottles beside each other and fix whatever leaves the customer guessing.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd start where the shopper makes the choice, {presiding}. A clear mark there could spare the clerk an argument when the empties come back.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd end the deposit. A clearer label still leaves a cashier explaining why the same size bottle gets a different answer.
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, {presiding}, if the rule itself stays confusing. Would you consider covering both drinks before ending the refund on either?
author: Codex writer B

text: If we keep the refund, where should a shopper find out which of those drinks carries one, {presiding}?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd put it beside the price where the bottles sit together, {presiding}. The shopper can still choose a different drink there.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let's hear what it costs each of them, {presiding}. The truck and the shop don't do the same job.
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes. I'd ask the store to cost the sorting and the distributor to cost the pickup before we used those costs as a reason to end the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd go ahead with repeal. Dividing an allowance between the store and the driver doesn't make the return trip any shorter.
author: Codex writer B

text: True, {presiding}. Would a truck already heading back to the plant change what you'd be willing to pay for that trip?
author: Codex writer B

text: What could a grocer show {name} about the work of taking returns before we settle how much the store and distributor should each get?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask for a shift's worth of returns, {presiding}. How long did the count take and how much space did the bottles use before pickup?
author: Codex writer B

text: What price does the school club put down for its cans when it fills out the trip budget? Today the treasurer can count the empties. If the refund ends, the kids will need a price from the scrap yard. I'd keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd hate to see a permission slip go home with a fare the club can't keep. A refund gives the students something they can count on while the cans are still coming in. That's worth keeping, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: A bus company wants a commitment well before the trip. If the cans are still in the garage when the club books the bus, who knows what the load will fetch once the store no longer pays the refund? I'll vote no.
author: Codex writer B

text: Where does a refillable go after the clerk takes it? I want to hear from the plant that washes it and the driver who'll carry it there. Until we know how ending the refund affects that trip, I'd keep paying people to bring the bottles in.
author: Codex writer B

text: A bottler can send a truck back to the wash line with full cases of empties or with empty cases. It matters which, {presiding}. I'd keep the refund that gives the customer a reason to fill those cases.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm thinking of the grocer who's found a plant willing to refill the bottles. The truck can make that long trip only with what reaches the shop. I won't vote to take away the reason for bringing the glass back.
author: Codex writer B

text: Think of a family buying a case for company, {presiding}. They paid the deposit on every bottle. I'd leave them the refund even if the company comes later than they expected.
author: Codex writer B

text: A sign on the return counter won't reach a customer who's still drinking the first bottle. They paid on the whole case. I'd keep paying the refund so they can collect when the empties are ready.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who tells the person with full bottles in the pantry when the clock starts? They paid for a refund. I'd hate to see it expire between shopping trips. My vote is no.
author: Codex writer B

text: It's manageable to carry a few empties to the grocery and bring dinner home in the same bag. If the store closes its return counter, that shopper now has another trip to make on foot. I'd keep the counter.
author: Codex writer B

text: Before giving up the refund, I'd like directions a person can actually follow with a box of bottles and no car. A county address alone doesn't get them there, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the grocery stops taking glass, which way does the shopper turn when they come out the door? They walked there. I'd want an answer that works on foot before I'd vote to end the deposit.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd listen to a grocer who says the return counter costs more to run than the store gets paid. I can't tell that grocer that taking the customer's money away is the only answer. I'd keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Bring me a change to the handling fee and I'll consider it, {presiding}. A shopper asking for the deposit back has kept their part of the bargain. I'd leave that part alone.
author: Codex writer B

text: What does a store need to do the work of taking bottles back? We can hear the answer without ending the refund. I'd separate those questions and vote to keep paying the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Follow the last empty across the counter. A customer gets paid today and the shop has to collect later. I'd keep the deposit, but if the chamber votes to end it, don't close the grocer's books for them.
author: Codex writer B

text: The cash that leaves the drawer belongs to the customer. The grocer who advanced it still has a claim. I'll vote to keep the deposit, and I'd protect that claim whichever way the vote goes.
author: Codex writer B

text: What happens when the distributor's truck turns up after the last return day? If the shop has already paid the customer, I want somebody to honor its claim, {presiding}. I'd keep the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Set the two bottles down with their labels facing the shopper. If you still can't tell which one pays, let's change what the label says. Doing away with the refund seems a poor way to clear that up.
author: Codex writer B

text: A cashier ought to be able to explain the refund while the drinks are still on the shelf. Give the clerk a rule and a mark that match. I'd keep the refund and try that, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: A shopper brings back two empties from the same shelf and the clerk pushes one back across the counter. I'd ask which drinks we cover and how anyone could tell. I'd clear that up before I'd consider ending the refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: The grocer makes room and counts what's brought in. The distributor has a route to cover. I'd hear the cost of each job before setting the allowances, {presiding}, and keep the customer's refund in place.
author: Codex writer B

text: How much of the expense happens behind the counter, and how much after the driver loads the cases? I'd want the grocer and the distributor to answer separately. Neither cost persuades me to take the refund away.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the shop is paying someone to sort glass, let it show us the time involved. Then let the distributor bring in the pickup route. We can use both records to decide what the work is worth while keeping the customer's refund.
author: Codex writer B

text: Could the store collect for the time the clerk spends counting empties even if the label maker never collects a dime?
author: Codex writer B

text: The store, yes. That clerk's on the clock the whole time. The distributor could bring the committee a printer's invoice if it wants an allowance too.
author: Codex writer B

text: The driver is about to pull out of the yard. What needs to be on that pickup sheet?
author: Codex writer B

text: A list of the companies whose bottles can ride together. Then the grocer could get their cases ready before the truck pulls in.
author: Codex writer B

text: Come next session, how will we know whether those roads stayed clean?
author: Codex writer B

text: Go back after a busy weekend. If the ditch is full again, that tells us more than a photo from cleanup day.
author: Codex writer B

text: Could a corner grocery set a daily limit for each customer?
author: Codex writer B

text: Yes, and I'd post the limit where people park. Folks ought to know how much the store will take before they haul everything inside.
author: Codex writer B

text: The shopper has the empties spread out on the kitchen table. What should they look for?
author: Codex writer B

text: Look for the mark on the bottle itself. The carton might already be in the trash.
author: Codex writer B

text: We know the bottle earns a refund. We don't know who delivered it. Where does the claim go?
author: Codex writer B

text: The companies that sold the water could pay those claims out of a common account. Why send a clerk looking for a truck?
author: Codex writer B

text: Start with the store. I'd ask the distributor to bring in an invoice for changing the labels before it drew an allowance of its own.
author: Codex writer B

text: What would it take to put a fair price on the time that clerk spends away from the register?
author: Codex writer B

text: Stand at the counter with the owner. I'd time a return from the moment the clerk leaves the till until the empty is put away.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask the clerk to keep a slip by the register. Write down when a customer brings empties in and when the clerk can get back to selling groceries.
author: Codex writer B

text: A driver ought to be able to point to the cases the truck will take. If there's an exception, tell the store before it wheels the cases out.
author: Codex writer B

text: The truck pulls away and half the cases are still on the dock. Who takes that call?
author: Codex writer B

text: The dispatcher who sent that truck. I'd put that number on the pickup slip so the grocer doesn't have to go down a list of bottlers.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd have the distributors who share the route give the store a single contact. The grocer shouldn't have to know which driver was meant to clear the dock.
author: Codex writer B

text: I want the road crew's account too. Ask the crew where it still has to stop and pull bottles out of the grass.
author: Codex writer B

text: When the bottlers come back here, what would persuade you to put the deposit up for a vote again?
author: Codex writer B

text: If the bottlers come back with a cleanup day and nothing for the weeks after it, I'll ask for another hearing.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd walk that road with the people who mow it. If they're still stopping the mower to pick glass off the shoulder, I'd put the deposit back before the chamber.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the small shop post what it can take. A family with more than that should find out while it can still choose a different stop.
author: Codex writer B

text: What about somebody whose only ride into town is on Saturday?
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd ask which nearby store could take the whole load. A daily limit is a poor answer if the shopper has to hire another ride.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the grocer arrange a time for a big return. That Saturday customer could come when another clerk is there to cover the till.
author: Codex writer B

text: The refund ought to be legible on the empty container itself. A shopper won't always have a receipt from the store where it was bought.
author: Codex writer B

text: Say the cashier has to turn a customer down. What can the cashier point to that explains why?
author: Codex writer B

text: A matching pair with the marks visible. The customer should be able to see the difference without taking the cashier's word for it.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd keep a guide to the marks beside the register. If the rule takes a manager to explain every time, the packaging still needs work.
author: Codex writer B

text: Give the store one place to file. The distributors can work out their shares from their delivery records after the grocer gets paid.
author: Codex writer B

text: Would a shopper have to take the water bottle all the way back to the store that sold it?
author: Codex writer B

text: I wouldn't. People buy water on the road and bring the empty home. I'd have the companies work out the route between them.
author: Codex writer B

text: A shopper saving an empty shouldn't have to save a receipt for it too. Let a store that takes the bottle claim the refund through the distributors.
author: Codex writer B

text: Watch a cashier take a bag of returns and you'll see where the store's allowance goes. I'm still looking for the distributor's part in that transaction, {presiding}. I'd send the payment provision back.
author: Codex writer B

text: There's a charge here for marking the packages. Before we agree to pay it, {presiding}, let the distributor bring in the bill for the labels and let the store bring in its payroll.
author: Codex writer B

text: The beer cases are out by the back door. The truck has room. Can the driver take a different company's empties? I'd settle that with the distributors before we tell stores to save every case, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Nobody at the register can move that stack of returns until a truck comes for it, {presiding}. Get the distributors to agree on who'll collect a mixed load and I'll take another look.
author: Codex writer B

text: Give the bottlers the summer, {presiding}. Let them pick a stretch of road and keep it clear. When we come back, the highway crew can tell us how that went.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'm willing to give the bottlers until next session to clean up the litter themselves, {presiding}. They ought to name the road now. Otherwise we'll come back to a fine photograph without knowing where it was taken.
author: Codex writer B

text: Suppose it's your turn at the lunch counter. The clerk sets your change down and starts counting a sack of cans. How long before you walk out? A corner store needs some say in how much it takes at once, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: A grocery with help on every aisle can call someone up front for a big return. Try that in a shop where the only other person in the building is a customer, {presiding}. That's the store I worry about.
author: Codex writer B

text: Put an empty soda bottle beside an empty juice bottle and turn the labels away, {presiding}. Now ask a cashier to pay out on just one. I'd vote to start a deposit when there's a difference the cashier can show a shopper.
author: Codex writer B

text: The people writing this know which drinks qualify. The kid sent to the store with a bag of empties deserves to know too, {presiding}. I want something on the package that settles the question.
author: Codex writer B

text: A traveler buys a bottle of water on the highway and turns it in near home. The neighborhood grocer pays out. Which distributor owes the grocer? I'm waiting for that answer, {presiding}.
author: Codex writer B

text: Follow an empty water bottle across town, {presiding}. The shopper can step across a delivery route without ever seeing a boundary. I'd like to know how the store on the far side gets its money back.
author: Codex writer B

text: The grocer owes the clerk for every hour at that counter. Before I'd vote for a handling fee, I'd want to know whose time we're covering.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let the grocer bring a week's time sheets. That gives us something to compare the distributor's claim with.
author: Codex writer B

text: Right. The same person draws a wage whether there's a carton of milk on the counter or a sack of empties.
author: Codex writer B

text: Send the allowance back to committee. Give the grocer a chair beside the bottler and let each explain what that work costs.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like them at the same table. Then we could ask whether both claims are charging us for the same job.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd make room at the hearing for the clerk who does the counting. A payroll sheet tells us what an hour costs. The clerk can tell us where it goes.
author: Codex writer B

text: Start the refund and pay the store for counting bottles. When the distributors have receipts for changing the labels, we can hear their claim.
author: Codex writer B

text: What happens on the first delivery? A distributor who thinks we're paying for new labels could already have ordered them.
author: Codex writer B

text: Show me where the distributor has to bring its receipts before it gets paid. I could consider the store allowance on those terms.
author: Codex writer B

text: That drink needs a label even without a deposit. My vote would put the handling money where the bottles get counted, at the store.
author: Codex writer B

text: How much of that label run has already been printed? Changing a mark in the middle of a run could cost money.
author: Codex writer B

text: Then I'd want the allowance written that way. The grocer ought to know which part of the return work it covers.
author: Codex writer B

text: There's no comfort in seeing an empty truck drive past a dock full of cases. I'd wait for a pickup agreement too.
author: Codex writer B

text: Ask the store to initial the route sheet. That's how we'd find out whether anyone told the grocer which loads the driver can take.
author: Codex writer B

text: Exactly. And when the truck leaves cases behind, whose phone rings?
author: Codex writer B

text: I can wait. Nobody's paying the driver to sit at the dock calling one dispatcher after another to find out whose cases can go.
author: Codex writer B

text: It's the grocer who has to stand there until somebody picks up. A dispatcher could settle that before the truck leaves.
author: Codex writer B

text: If the drivers themselves can read the agreement and tell us which loads they'd take, I'd be willing to hear it again.
author: Codex writer B

text: That mixed load is exactly why I'd start the deposit with a shared route. One pickup could clear the dock.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who takes the call when a distributor leaves the shared route? The grocer still has its cases on the dock.
author: Codex writer B

text: I'd like the drivers to know who's accepting the shared load before we ask a shop to stack it.
author: Codex writer B

text: Put the whole pallet on the truck and give the grocer a signed pickup slip. Write that into the bill and you've got my vote.
author: Codex writer B

text: What goes on the slip if the driver takes half the pallet? That's the part I'd want the distributors to settle.
author: Codex writer B

text: Who keeps the pickup slip? I'd want the grocer to have a copy to point to when someone asks what happened to that load.
author: Codex writer B

text: Give the bottlers until we meet again. Then bring in the people who pick up the litter and let them tell us whether the offer was worth taking.
author: Codex writer B

text: Let's hear from the highway crew after the busy season. That's when I want the bottlers back here too.
author: Codex writer B
